project.rawInput: Working title: Run Your Morality as a Unit Test. Why do people selectively apply moral standards to salient companies and people? Test equivalent cases with names removed, investigate MSNBC/Gates ownership, Tesla versus Volkswagen and alcohol/drug policy without assuming these comparisons hold. Generate the first complete evidence-grounded Tim White essay and vlog episode.

wardrobe.rule: Only reference approved outfits from the global collection; never invent wardrobe or biographical facts.

plan.question: When we judge similar behavior differently, are we protecting a principle, responding to a meaningful difference, or giving our favorite side a pass?
hypotheses: Identity and familiarity influence moral judgment: removing names may change which conduct people excuse.
Apparently equivalent cases differ in relevant ways, including harm, intent, control, and available alternatives. Different judgments may be consistent.
Uneven attention reflects limited time or perceived influence rather than different moral standards.
The proposed comparisons may depend on mistaken ownership claims or mismatched evidence. Correcting those premises could weaken the thesis.
A names-removed test may expose favoritism, but it can also remove context needed for a fair judgment.
queries: What do blinded experiments show about political or brand identity changing moral judgments of identical conduct, and what findings challenge that effect?

What ownership or funding relationships, if any, connect Bill Gates to MSNBC, historically and today? Distinguish MSNBC from NBC, Microsoft, and grants to other news organizations using primary records.

Which specific Tesla and Volkswagen actions are being compared? Compare documented conduct, executive responsibility, harms, remedies, and evidence of public reactions before treating the cases as equivalent.

How do alcohol and other drug policies compare when accounting for dose, health harms, dependence, impairment, and enforcement costs? What evidence supports different treatment, and what suggests inconsistency?

sources.title: Preregistered replication and extension of Moral Hypocrisy: Social Groups and the Flexibility of Virtue
sources.evidence: The 2024 study reports two experiments with US Prolific participants. The original finding did not replicate, although the researchers observed in-group favoritism in minimal groups and out-group derogation in political groups. The authors describe the evidence as mixed and dependent on context.

sources.title: NBC News acquires full ownership of Msnbc Digital Network
sources.evidence: NBC's July 2012 announcement identifies Microsoft as the seller of a 50 percent interest in the digital joint venture. It distinguishes the digital properties from MSNBC television. The announcement does not identify Bill Gates as the personal owner.

sources.title: Versant Media Group 2025 Form 10-K
sources.evidence: The filing identifies MS NOW among Versant's networks and states that MSNBC's rebranding as MS NOW became effective in November 2025.

sources.title: Volkswagen agrees to plead guilty and pay criminal and civil penalties
sources.evidence: DOJ's January 2017 announcement describes Volkswagen's agreement to plead guilty to three felonies involving emissions-test cheating, obstruction, and false import statements. It reports $4.3 billion in criminal and civil penalties and an independent compliance monitor. Individual indictments were allegations.

sources.title: NHTSA opening resume for Tesla recall query RQ24009
sources.evidence: The April 2024 document opens an inquiry into the adequacy of Tesla's Autopilot recall remedy. It describes concerns about controls addressing driver misuse, mode confusion, and operation outside the system's intended environments. This is an investigation-opening document.

sources.title: WHO alcohol fact sheet
sources.evidence: WHO describes alcohol as toxic and dependence-producing. It identifies cancer and other health risks, while explaining that risk varies with consumption patterns and individual circumstances. Most alcohol-related harms arise from heavy episodic or heavy continuous consumption.

sources.title: WHO cannabis overview
sources.evidence: WHO identifies impaired coordination and attention, cannabis dependence, and respiratory harms associated with smoking. This overview supports broad risk categories, rather than a precise contemporary comparison across products, doses, or populations.

sources.title: Effects of marijuana legalization on law enforcement and crime
sources.evidence: The June 2020 Washington State study summary reports fewer people processed for nonviolent marijuana possession and no consistently positive or negative overall effects. Qualitative findings identify concerns about traffic safety, youth access, and interstate trafficking. Possible resource-allocation benefits are presented cautiously.

draft.title: The comparison has to earn its place
draft.essay:
The comparison needs a test too.

Before calling something a double standard, I want to know whether the two cases belong next to each other. Two folders labeled “car company did something bad” leave quite a lot out. My proposed starting rule: compare the conduct and evidence before comparing the verdicts. [C5]

Take Volkswagen and Tesla. The selected Volkswagen record describes an agreement to plead guilty over emissions cheating, obstruction, and false import statements. The Tesla document opens an inquiry into whether an Autopilot recall remedy was adequate. Different conduct. Different legal stages. Those records do not establish equivalent wrongdoing or show how comparable audiences reacted. [C4][C5]

That changes the question. What relevant difference would justify a different judgment? And would we accept that explanation with the company names swapped? That is the consistency test I would use. [C8]

There is a credible reason to investigate favoritism. A preregistered replication and extension found some group effects, but the original finding did not replicate. Results varied with context. That supports a limited claim that group identity can affect judgments, not a diagnosis of everyone who reaches a different conclusion. The experiments did not test these company comparisons. [C1]

So favoritism stays on the list of possible explanations. It has not earned the starring role. [C1][C5]

The strongest objection to covering the logos is that names can carry relevant context. Responsibility, history, and intent may matter. Removing them can make the comparison worse. I would cover the names for a first pass, then restore the context and identify the fact that changes the verdict. A changed answer should prompt examination, not an automatic hypocrisy charge. [C8]

Sometimes the premise needs repair before that exercise can even begin.

“Bill Gates owns MSNBC” is unsupported by this record. Microsoft's historical connection was real: it sold its half of the Msnbc digital joint venture in 2012. That announcement distinguishes the digital properties from the television channel. It does not establish Gates's personal ownership or control over editorial decisions. Corporate ownership, personal ownership, funding, and editorial control need separate evidence. [C2]

The alcohol and cannabis comparison needs a similar repair. Both carry documented health risks. These sources do not establish a universal ranking of harm per person, dose, or occasion. Familiarity does not supply the missing comparison, and neither does enthusiasm for legalization. [C6]

Policy adds another question: what happens under a particular set of rules? A Washington State study reported fewer people processed for nonviolent marijuana possession, without consistently positive or negative overall effects. It also recorded qualitative concerns about traffic safety, youth access, and interstate trafficking. Those concerns are not equivalent to measured increases in harm, and one jurisdiction does not settle policy everywhere. [C7]

I would keep those questions separate: the health risks, the effects of enforcement, and the outcomes we want policy to prioritize. That last part requires a value judgment as well as evidence.

For now, I would write down the conduct, the evidence, and the rule. Cover the names, make a first judgment, then put the context back. If the answer changes, explain why. The useful test is whether that reason survives the names being swapped, while preserving differences that actually matter. It is a reasoning practice, not a validated cure for bias. [C8]

spoken.text: The comparison needs a test too. Before I call something a double standard, I want to check whether the cases actually belong next to each other. That's the standard I'm proposing.

Take Volkswagen and Tesla. In the records here, Volkswagen agreed to plead guilty over emissions cheating and related conduct. The Tesla document opened an inquiry into whether its Autopilot recall fix was adequate. Two folders labeled “car company did something bad” leave quite a lot out.

Those are different legal stages and different conduct. These records also don't show how comparable audiences reacted. So the accusation of a double standard is still unproven. I'd start by asking which differences should matter.

Favoritism is worth investigating. But the research here is mixed. A preregistered replication and extension found some group effects, while the original finding didn't replicate. The results depended on context. That gives us a possibility to examine, not an explanation for every disagreement.

My first pass would be to cover the names and write down the rule. Then put the context back. And there's a fair objection: the context might matter. History, responsibility, intent. If one of those changes the answer, explain how. A changed verdict doesn't automatically prove hypocrisy.

Before doing that, though, check the premise. “Bill Gates owns MSNBC” isn't supported here. Microsoft sold its half of the Msnbc digital joint venture in 2012. That record distinguishes the digital business from television. It doesn't establish Gates's personal ownership or editorial control.

Alcohol and cannabis need some care too. Both have documented health risks. These sources don't give us one universal harm ranking across doses, products, and people. I'd want the comparison to specify what harm we're measuring.

Then there's the policy question. A Washington State study reported fewer people processed for nonviolent marijuana possession, without consistently positive or negative overall effects. It also recorded safety concerns. Those concerns weren't themselves proof that harms increased. That's a qualified result, and it doesn't settle every jurisdiction.

Where I land is pretty provisional. Write down what happened, what evidence we have, and which rule applies. Restore the context after the first pass. If your answer changes, name the fact that changed it. Then ask whether you'd accept that reason with the names swapped. I'd use that to start an investigation.

A source-checking moment around the Microsoft transaction, following the distinction between the digital venture and television.
A natural break in the conversation to consider which fact would legitimately change the judgment once the names return.
